source.title: Concept-Guided Interpretability via Neural Chunking
source.authors: Shu-Chen Wu; S. Alaniz; Shyamgopal Karthik; Peter Dayan; Eric Schulz; Zeynep Akata

record.tranche_reason: Extends evidence about distributed concept representations to large language models, using neural population chunk measurements rather than the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper measures concept-related neural population activity and its ability to predict concepts. Its grafting and freezing results are purposefully induced behavior, so they are not evidence for the claim versions about naturally arising feature geometry. The paper's statements about polysemantic neurons in related work cite prior studies and are not recorded as results here.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is a new interpretability method (neural chunking), not superposition. Its one result bearing on a version is a side observation in LLaMA-3-8B (SI E.1): concepts are encoded by substantial neural populations, and sparse encodings are rare. That is a different method bearing on V4's 'features spread across many neurons' clause. The decoding and grafting results measure the method's own performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' central claim is the 'Reflection Hypothesis': population activity mirrors regularities in training data. Chunking methods (DSC, PA, UCD) extract chunks correlating with words, POS tags and narrative schemas, and grafting or freezing them causally shifts outputs. The distributed-population point is a supplementary remark, not a headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses discrete sequence chunking, population averaging, and unsupervised chunk discovery to identify recurring population activity; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: PA performance depends on concept type and context: the authors report better results for specific-meaning words than prepositions, and note that contextually nuanced words can correspond to distinct chunks. Grafting effectiveness also varies by intervention layer and prompt category, but those induced effects do not test these claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: PA chunk detection predicts word occurrence on held-out prompts with low false positives across LLaMA-3, T5, RWKV and Mamba. This is weaker for prepositions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept-related population activity is recoverable by averaging-based prototypes (method performance).

fits_no_version.finding: PA chunks decode three selected words better than the most active SAE latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Population prototypes outperform single SAE latents as concept detectors.

fits_no_version.finding: Grafting PA chunks raises concept occurrence, e.g. cake 1%→83%, with early layers most effective. Freezing lowers it, e.g. cheese 67%→33%.

record.problems: The distributed-population result is stated qualitatively, with numerical layer-wise values shown only in figures. The concept measurements use selected concepts and prompt sets; the authors note that performance can be weaker for prepositions and other context-sensitive words. The paper does not test superposition geometry or capacity competition.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the tested version. Grafting and freezing outcomes, narrative-chunk results, and RNN results were left out because they do not measure the LLM feature distribution or SAE recovery named by V4.

untested.parts: No toy models of superposition, sparsity transition or geometry. The RNN experiments test recurring trajectories, not superposition.
Capacity competition is not tested. Polysemanticity is mentioned only via cited work.
No result on non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAE recovery of sparse features is not tested. The SAE comparison is method-versus-method decoding on three words.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. The authors only remark that SAE features map indirectly to words.
The dimensionality of features is not tested. Chunks are defined as bounded balls, not directions, but this is a definitional choice, not a result.

missing.what: Number of concept-encoding neurons across layers for Mamba, T5 and RWKV. This is the same distribution measure as r1, in other architectures.

Memory of a past signal is represented much more sparsely than the current signal, and a smaller population predicts future tokens. This shows that the degree of distribution depends on token position.

record.verdict_notes: Weak test of V4. The only relevant evidence is one qualitative sentence in SI E.1, whose neuron counts depend on the PA tolerance hyperparameter. Distributed encoding is consistent with superposition but does not establish it. The original source (Toy Models) is cited only in related work. The reader's labels wrongly used method-performance rows (r2–r6) as evidence for V4.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for limited capacity causes polysemanticity or assigns dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study measures distributed population activity for concepts and compares it with SAE concept-neuron decoding on selected concepts; it does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or generally recoverable.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of a model's representation.
Whether the features implicated in superposition are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the number of neurons contributing to population-averaged concept chunks across layers.

conditions.value: concepts analyzed with PA; examples include words

rows.measure: Number of neurons contributing to recurring concept-related embedding activity; whether concepts are encoded sparsely or by populations.
rows.value: Concept encoding is generally supported by substantial populations of neurons rather than isolated units; sparse encodings of concepts are rare.
rows.note: The paper states the qualitative result; layer-wise numerical values are presented in figures but are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Qualitative statement only; per-layer neuron counts are figure-only (Figs 14–17). The neuron count C(s) is set by the method's tolerance threshold, so 'distributed' partly depends on a method choice. Baseline 'isolated units' is a framing, not a measured control.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated PA chunks by testing whether chunk detection predicts concept occurrence on held-out neural recordings.
rows.measure: Concept decoding performance, shown as average performance across words.
rows.note: The text says PA chunks consistently correspond to meaningful concepts and reliably predict associated concepts with minimal false positives; exact plotted values are not provided in the supplied text.
rows.check: This is the study's own method's decoding performance (PA chunk TPR/FPR). It measures how well the method detects concepts, not whether the model's features are distributed or superposed.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared PA concept-chunk decoding with decoding by the most active concept-related SAE neurons.

conditions.value: selected concepts, including cheese, cake, and cheesecake

rows.measure: Prediction of selected concept occurrence from internal activity.
rows.value: PA-extracted population activity predicts the selected concept better than the individual concept neurons identified by SAE.
rows.note: The comparison is reported qualitatively; the supplied text gives no exact decoding values.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (PA) against single SAE latents for three selected words. This is method versus method on cheese/cake/cheesecake, and does not test whether SAEs recover sparse features. Text gives no numbers.

rows.subject: T5 (t5-small)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whether PA-extracted concept chunks predict concepts on held-out neural recordings.
rows.note: The paper reports generalization to T5 and presents example-concept evaluation in the figure; exact plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Method decoding performance on T5. It does not measure feature distribution, and the figure-only values are unreadable here.

rows.subject: rwkv-4-169m-pile
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whether PA-extracted concept chunks predict concepts on held-out neural recordings.
rows.note: The paper reports generalization to RWKV and presents example-concept evaluation in the figure; exact plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Method decoding performance on RWKV. It does not measure feature distribution.

rows.subject: mamba-130m-hf
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whether PA-extracted concept chunks predict concepts on held-out neural recordings.
rows.note: The paper reports generalization to Mamba and presents example-concept evaluation in the figure; exact plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Method decoding performance on Mamba. It does not measure feature distribution.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-3-8B residual stream, PA-extracted concept subpopulations (e.g. cake, in, of, people)
relationships.reason: r1: authors report concepts supported by substantial neuron populations and sparse encodings are rare. This is qualitative and dependent on PA tolerance.
relationships.display_finding: The authors report that concepts are supported by substantial neuron populations and that sparse encodings are rare. The evidence is qualitative and depends on the PA tolerance setting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
